source: Song et al. (2025) Is a Peeled Apple Still Red? Conceptual combination with property types (CCPT), arXiv 2502.06086, table re-read
finding: Re-read of Table 3 against the paper text. The text says GPT-4o with spreading activation plus ConceptNet scores 12.3 points above gold on relatedness to the parts (R_H,M,P) and 1.6 points below gold on relatedness to the phrase (R_N,P). That matches the fourth GPT-4o row (41.5 vs gold 29.2; 85.8 vs 87.4), not the fifth. So the rows run: Base, CoT, S.A. with LLM, S.A. with ConceptNet, S.A. with both, then the gray Multi-Oracle row (best of N=5 samples, an upper bound, not a method). The earlier critique reading shifted every label by one row and took the Multi-Oracle row as the scaffold result.
numbers: GPT-4o emergent-property score E, property induction: Base 40.8, CoT 42.4, S.A. with LLM 43.8, S.A. with ConceptNet 45.8, S.A. with both 45.2, Multi-Oracle 57.8 (gold 58.4, human 49.2). So the scaffold gain is about +5.0 points and CoT about +1.6, not +15. Noun-phrase completion E: Base 20.4, CoT 23.1, S.A. LLM 25.5, S.A. ConceptNet 26.9, S.A. both 26.8, Multi-Oracle 38.9 (human 38.0, gold 59.9). Human property-type accuracy 81% vs GPT-4o 56.4%. Judge-vs-human agreement checked on 300 pairs (Figure 4, MTurk raters). Human eval N=30 per Table 4.
limits: Row mapping is an inference from two numbers in the text (12.3 and 1.6) that both fit one row; it is also consistent with o1 and Sonnet having only two rows (Base and Multi-Oracle). Judge is an LLM. Best-of-5 sampling alone (Multi-Oracle) gives about +17 points, far more than any scaffold.
agent_relevance: The 57.8 figure is an oracle over 5 samples. Sampling several candidates and picking with a good check is worth far more than a spreading-activation scaffold, which fits the generate-many-then-filter shape of O7. Do not cite +15 for the scaffold.

source: Kennedy (2015) Univ. of Alabama thesis, emergence effects in story word choice; with Ward, Kennedy and Kaufman (2013) as cited there
finding: Atypical (anomalous) concept pairs did not make stories more creative, a failure to replicate the idea that far pairs raise creative output. The earlier Ward et al. 2013 study also found no coder-rated creativity gain. Atypical seeds changed word use (more verbs, auxiliary verbs, adverbs) in both studies.
numbers: N=195 students (typical vs atypical seeds, 3 pairs each: Enemy, Sky, Death). Coder ratings by condition: total F(1,193)=1.680 p>.05; Enemy F=.016; Sky F(1,193)=4.446 p<.05 (modest). Coder reliability low: Cronbach alpha .656 (Enemy), .599 (Sky), .632 (Death). LIWC: auxiliary verbs F(1,193)=16.127 p<.001; adverbs F(1,193)=10.937 p<.001; common verbs F(1,193)=4.586 p<.05. Creativity measures (Alternate Uses Task r=.022) did not predict story performance.
limits: Student sample, story writing not problem solving, rater reliability below target, so a null is weak evidence. Agrees with Chan, Dow and Schunn (d03) that distance does not buy quality.
agent_relevance: Do not assume far input pairs give better outputs. Measure validity and usefulness per distance bin.

source: Chan, Dow and Schunn (2015; open chapter 2018) Do the best design ideas (really) come from conceptually distant sources of inspiration? Design Studies 36
finding: On an open innovation platform, ideas that cited sources were more often shortlisted by expert judges, but the benefit came from near sources. Far sources gave about the same shortlist rate as citing nothing. The inverse relation of distance to creativity held across the challenges.
numbers: 2,341 concepts, 4,557 inspirations, 12 design challenges; main sample 707 concepts that cited inspirations, 110 (about 16%) shortlisted. Distance by LDA topic model (400 topics); LDA cosine vs human distance rating r=0.51 (95% CI .40 to .60), above best human-human r=.48. Max distance coefficient -0.33 log-odds per unit (95% CI -0.06 to -0.60), p<.05. Predicted shortlist for no-citation concepts 0.09 (95% CI .07 to .11); any-citation coefficient 0.31 (CI .01 to .62). Between-challenge variance about zero.
limits: Observational field data, outcome is shortlist status (expert judged), distance from the problem not between two blend inputs. A moderate-distance sweet spot is not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Prefer near or mid-distance partners for the open-mode blend, and treat far pairs as a costly gamble that needs a validity check.

source: Chan and Schunn (2015) The impact of analogies on creative concept generation: lessons from an in vivo study in engineering design, Cognitive Science 39
finding: In a professional design team's brainstorming, concepts after a far analogy were more similar to the preceding concept than at baseline, not less. But far analogies raised the team's concept generation rate. So far analogies did not work through big jumps; they worked through steady deeper exploration.
numbers: Abstract only (Crossref): no numbers read. Single professional team, conversation transcripts.
limits: Abstract only; paywalled. One team. Supports the claim on iteration (K10) only indirectly.
agent_relevance: A blend step may pay off through the follow-up elaboration rounds, not through the first combination.

source: Estes and Ward (2002) The emergence of novel attributes in concept modification, Creativity Research Journal 14
finding: Seen only in the abstract via a search summary. Irrelevant or atypical modifiers produced more emergent attributes; relevance and typicality were inversely related to emergence; antonymous and anomalous pairings gave the most.
limits: Abstract only; full text not accessible this session. Number of participants and counts unknown.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that incongruent inputs force emergence, but quality was not measured here.

source: Wilkenfeld and Ward (2001) Similarity and emergence in conceptual combination, J Memory and Language 45; via Kennedy (2015) description
finding: Described by Kennedy: pairs that are hard to align (motorcycle carpet) gave more emergent properties than pairs that align easily (guitar harp). A search summary says the same: similar pairs gave fewer emergent features than dissimilar ones.
numbers: No numbers read. Publisher abstract withheld (Semantic Scholar shows the abstract elided).
limits: Second-hand; paywalled. Counts of emergent features per condition not obtained.
agent_relevance: Same as d05. Emergence rises with misalignment, but valid-and-useful emergence was not scored.

source: Peeperkorn, Kouwenhoven, Brown, Jordanous (2024) Is temperature the creativity parameter of large language models? arXiv 2405.00492
finding: With one fixed model and prompt, temperature has only a weak positive link to rated novelty and a moderate link to incoherence. No link to cohesion or typicality. Not a creativity knob.
numbers: Llama-2-chat 70B (quantised). 100 stories at each of 7 temperatures (0.001 to 2.0) for the computational analysis. Human study: 36 participants, 31 stories (about 5 unique per temperature), each rater 5 stories. Mixed model: novelty beta=.308 (SE .138, p<.05); coherence beta=.240 (SE .122, p<.05); typicality and cohesion n.s. Perplexity vs novelty beta=.730 (SE .273).
limits: One model, one story prompt, non-expert raters, small N, story writing not blending. It says nothing about the generic-space step.
agent_relevance: Raising temperature will not repair a bad bridge choice. A hotter sample buys a little novelty and costs coherence; use distinct retries with a check instead of a hotter single pass. KOMBINE's temperature 0.9 is not a tested optimum.

source: Fujiyoshi (2026) From theory to protocol: executable frameworks for creative emergence and strategic foresight, arXiv 2604.09597
finding: The closest thing found to the missing arm. A 5-step collision protocol (strip labels from two domains, extract shared structure, collide) was compared with plain brainstorming on the same inputs and the same model (Claude). Protocol output scored higher in one blind case. Token cost was not matched or reported as equal.
numbers: Case study D, blind evaluation by a separate AI session: protocol 74/80 vs brainstorming 49/80 (author scores 75/80 vs 64/80). Batch of 8 random domain pairings: 7 of 8 judged successes (87.5%). Author-defined rubric and success criterion. Single operator.
limits: One case for the head-to-head, an AI judge, author-written rubric and protocol, N=8 batch with no baseline arm. The author states human blind raters are still needed. Weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Shows the structured arm can be run cheaply and gives a template, but does not close gap 1. Our own test must use equal tokens and a code or human check.

source: Wang and Luan (2026) Toward auto-research: mining falsifiable research ideas from paper knowledge graphs with categorical structure, arXiv 2608.20361
finding: A published code-based structural check on cross-domain bridges: a functor-preservation gate computes how many typed relations of the source map to relations of the target. It runs before an LLM judge and is cheap. It is the nearest published analogue of checking a generic frame by code.
numbers: Gate thresholds: preservation F below 0.30 rejected, 0.30 to 0.60 speculative, above accepted. Funnel: 13,951 gate-passed in the full set, 163 cross-domain judged candidates, 9 survivors (judge threshold 0.30, six axes). Gate filters cross-domain candidates about 17:1. Quantitative-falsifier rate of accepted ideas 83.4 to 88.9% across four conditions. 154 rejected vs 9 survivors separate on every judge axis. Each LLM judgment about 103 output tokens.
limits: Authors say they have not measured false negatives against a held-out human-graded set. Checks typed graph structure extracted from papers, not free-text frames. The six-axis judge is an LLM and runs fail-open (null counts as pass).
agent_relevance: Shows the shape of a code check (types match, relations preserved) but gives no agreement with humans. Gap 3 stays open: no measured human agreement exists for any generic-frame checker.

source: Yu, He, Ying (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.03965
finding: Solve analogous problems first, then reuse their solutions. This is analogy, not blending, but it has hard task outcomes, which blend studies lack.
numbers: Shortest-path reasoning +12% absolute optimal solutions; creative writing +13% human preference; LLM-agent planning +15% task completion (vs baselines, abstract only).
limits: Abstract only; baselines not named; transfer of solutions, no emergent structure from two inputs.
agent_relevance: Evidence that structured use of analogues improves task results. It does not show that blending two inputs does.

source: Zahn, Evans, Eagleman (2026) Discovery by dreaming: cross-domain recombination in artificial memory, arXiv 2607.16256
finding: Cross-domain recombination, done as LoRA training on mixed-domain material, improved gold-answer task accuracy. Within-domain rehearsal did nothing. Prepending the same material in context to a 671B model did not reproduce the gain and reversed it.
numbers: Neural arm +5.64 pp overall (p=.0055); GSM8K +14.5 pp headline; at rank 256 on the full 1,319-item test all 5 seeds positive, bootstrap 95% CI +9.8 to +18.7; gold-answer tasks need no LLM judge (Llama-3.1-8B, n=5 seeds). Symbolic arm 85.7% novel cross-domain connections, +21 pp over a similarity baseline; Spearman 0.54 (n=32) between field distance and bridge rank.
limits: It is a training method, not a prompting operator, so it does not test a blend step in a scaffold. Some outcomes are judged by Qwen-72B; absolute accuracy shifts about 15 points by judge.
agent_relevance: One of the few cross-domain recombination results with a task outcome. The in-context reversal warns that stuffing a second domain into the prompt can hurt.

source: Radensky et al. (2024) Scideator: human-LLM compound system for scientific ideation through facet recombination and novelty evaluation, arXiv 2409.14634
finding: Facet recombination (user picks purpose and mechanism facets from different papers, system finds analogies) gave researchers more creativity support than the same LLM without the facet modules. Outcome is a rated support score, not task success.
numbers: Abstract only: significant gain in creativity support in a user study with CS researchers; no effect sizes in the abstract. Facet-grounded novelty classifier beat classifiers on unstructured text.
limits: Abstract only; self-rated support; human in the loop.
agent_relevance: Structured facets before recombining beat unstructured use of the same model, on user ratings. Another rating, not a task outcome.

source: Li, Carlson, Potts (2022) Systematicity in GPT-3's interpretation of novel English noun compounds, arXiv 2210.09492
finding: GPT-3 interpretations of novel noun-noun compounds match human interpretation patterns from Levin et al. 2019 (artifact vs natural-kind modifier effects). But when nonce words are defined as artifacts or natural kinds (Experiment 3), GPT-3 is much less successful, so the match may rest on word-level statistics, not on concept-level reasoning.
numbers: Human relation-type shares by compound class: artifact-artifact (e.g. stew skillet) 93% / 7% / 0% over three coded types (N=195); natural-natural 15% / 34% / 51% (N=148). Three experiments, four temperature settings.
limits: GPT-3 only (2022). Compound interpretation, not emergent-property generation.
agent_relevance: An LLM-era check of Hampton-style conceptual combination. The nonce-word failure is a caution: a plausible blend may only reflect word frequency.

source: Ciapparelli, Zarbo, Marelli (2025) Conceptual combination in large language models: uncovering implicit relational interpretations in compound words with contextualized word embeddings, Cognitive Science (DOI 10.1111/cogs.70048)
finding: BERT-base and Llama-2-13b embeddings of a compound shift when it is replaced by its implicit-relation paraphrase, and the shift tracks human plausibility ratings. The pattern is much weaker for novel compounds, where older distributional models do better.
numbers: Abstract only (via Crossref); no numbers read.
limits: Abstract only; embedding analysis, not generation; models are small or older.
agent_relevance: Novel combinations are where LLMs track humans least well. Do not trust a model's judgment of a new blend without an external check.

source: Lynn (2026) Conceptual blending in humans and language models, Frontiers in Psychology, PMC13461484
finding: A conceptual analysis with a toy vector-symbolic model; no LLM blending experiments and no results table. It names goals as the selector of which affordances get blended and treats LLM blends as steered by proxy goals from prompt framing. Cites Peng 2025 and Sato 2025 without reporting their findings.
limits: Position paper. Does not answer gap 9 or gap 2.
agent_relevance: Supports giving the blend operator an explicit goal (K23), as a design idea only.

source: Schapiro et al. (2025/26) KOMBINE abstract page, arXiv 2509.21043 (re-checked for gap 5)
finding: The abstract page reports no temperature, retry or second-model repair test. It does say models reuse properties invented by other models more for blends than analogies, and more within the same provider. So a second model from another provider is more likely to add different properties, but nobody has measured whether it repairs the 43.4% generic-space step.
numbers: 35 LLMs, 75 humans. No temperature sweep reported on the page.
limits: Abstract page only for this check; body numbers are in evidence_a, b and c. The statement about repair is an inference.
agent_relevance: Test cross-family retry on the generic frame step in our own harness; treat it as untested.

source: Gibbs (2000) Making good psychology out of blending theory; Coulson and Matlock (2001); McCubbins and Turner (2013); Eppe et al. (2018): access attempt
finding: All four sources were behind paywalls or blocked (403) this session, so none was opened. Crossref gave no abstracts for them. Gibbs's critique is already recorded second-hand through Ritchie (a08). No blending-specific experiment with numbers was found for any of the four.
limits: Not opened. Absence of numbers here is an access result, not evidence that the papers have none.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. Do not cite experiments from these four.

source: Xi, Cheng, Soni, Turner (2026) Evaluating creative generative AI with conceptual blending (poster); title searches for optimality-principle scoring
finding: Re-checked for gap 9. The poster proposes scoring by frames present, integration and emergent meaning, with no results. arXiv title searches on blending, bisociation, combinational creativity and conceptual combination (about 80 listed titles, 2010 to 2026) turned up no paper that scores unpacking or topology of an LLM blend and correlates it with human value ratings.
numbers: No results reported by the poster. Search limited by rate limits on arXiv and Semantic Scholar; the WebSearch quota was exhausted.
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search. Not exhaustive.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open as far as this search can say.

source: Search-limits note for gaps 7 and 8: Hampton replications 2010 to 2026 and expert case studies
finding: Titles found for Hampton-style work in the LLM era: Song et al. 2025 (CCPT, d01), Li et al. 2022 (d13), Ciapparelli et al. 2025 (d14). The quantum-cognition line (Aerts and others, arXiv 2009 to 2014, guppy effect) models Hampton-type conjunction data but is theory fitting, not a replication. No direct replication of Hampton's emergence counts was found. No design or science case study with an explicit generic-space step was found.
numbers: Humans on CCPT: emergent property induction E 49.2, noun-phrase completion E 38.0, property-type accuracy 81% (from d01).
limits: Absence from a rate-limited search. Hampton's own later work (2011 and after) was not reachable. The quantum-cognition titles were seen only as listings.
agent_relevance: The only current human baseline for emergence in conceptual combination found is CCPT's.
